nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
September 3, 1993.  T.D. Phillips; Mote Marine Laboratory

FLELMR Code: 1609

Common Name: Bluefish
Scientific Name: Pomatomus saltatrix
Other Common Names: blue (664); greenfish, tailor, snapping mackerel (312 834); snapper (51); skipjack (834); elf, fatback, snap mackerel, horse mackerel, skip mackerel, chopper, Hatteras blue (766 1392).

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
Class:     Osteichthyes
Order:   Perciformes
Family:  Pomatomidae

nodes.title: Value
nodes.body:
Commercial: Considered an incidental commercial species with most catches occurring in offshore waters (30 47 420). They were once common enough to support a small fishery in east Texas waters, but not since the 1930`s (255 320). In Alabama they are a relatively minor component of that state`s commercial fishery (694). Catches there are largely by trammel nets in waters off the Gulf beaches, but in recent years shrimp trawls have made up 25% of the catch (694). Statewide Florida landings in 1989 were 1,250,718 lbs worth approximately $318,249, and of that total, almost 67% were landed at Florida east coast ports (902). Catches are also made by pound nets, gill nets, purse seines, long haul seines, beach seines, and hook and line in other areas of the range of this fish (753 791 834). Marketed mostly fresh (791).

Recreational: An important sport species in both U.S. and Mexican waters. Its recreational importance far outweighs its commercial value especially on the Atlantic seaboard (30 47 420 304 695). Their voracity makes them an exciting game fish and they are also an excellent food fish (51 327). The recreational catch for 1991 for the Florida Gulf was estimated as 430,000 fish, and on the Florida Atlantic coast as 856,000 fish (1363). Angling methods include surf casting; hook and line fishing from piers, docks, bridges, and jetties; and trolling, casting, live bait fishing, and chumming from boats (51 753).

Ecological Role: A marine, high trophic level, pelagic predator that is primarily a visual feeder (518 520 766). Follow schools of small fishes into shallow water and are known to have bitten bathers (788 1406).

Indicator: Bluefish bioaccumulate contaminants such as polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB) from the water column and through the marine food chain into various adipose tissues (618). Studies by the National Marine Fisheries Service, the Food and Drug Administration, and the Environmental Protection Agency have found concentrations of PCBs in large bluefish that exceed the limit of 2 pg/g set by the Food & Drug Administration. This has prompted investigation to determine if states with bluefish fisheries need to control the consumption of large individuals to recreational and subsistence fishermen who regularly eat these fish ( 618 ) .

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body: Overall: Worldwide in distribution (327 766 788 791 887 891). In the western Atlantic from Nova Scotia to Argentina, and widespread in the Gulf of Mexico to Texas and Mexico (420 766 791). It is also found off Cuba, Bermuda, and the Azores (791 891). Rare or absent between south Florida and northern South America (788). Much less abundant overall in the Gulf of Mexico than in the Atlantic, and generally less common on the western side of the Gulf than the eastern (753).

nodes.title: By State
nodes.body:
Within Study Area: Occurs on both coasts of Florida (327 581 789 791 887 891). Abundant along the northeast Florida coast (1392) and common in winter and spring in the Jupiter Inlet area (887).  Caught offshore in the Gulf during most of the year (6641, and known to occur in relatively large numbers offshore of Cedar Key (581). Not common on the Florida west coast during the winter (581). Historically, known to be common near Pensacola (978).

Movements and Migrations
Adults: move seasonally in groups loosely collected into aggregates (766) that can be 6-8 km long ( 5 1 ) . Adults generally move north in spring and summer, and south in fall and winter (766 481). Long distance migrations from New York to Cuba, and from Virginia to the Florida Gulf coast have been documented ( 5 1 275). Florida blue fish remain in Florida waters until spring and large numbers are still found off southern Florida in March; some are present throughout the year (177 553 327 664). In the Gulf of Mexico, they remain offshore during much of the year moving inshore during the summer in Louisiana, late summer and fall in Mississippi, and fall in Florida and the northwestern Gulf. Seasonal migrations appear to be linked to water temperature and possibly photoperiod (519 766). Fall migration appears to be triggered when temperatures fall to 13-150 C. Adults are pelagic fish and move offshore to find warmer water in which to overwinter (421 766 581). Movements between offshore and inshore
waters are irregular and may be a response to wind induced changes in water temperature (421 766 581).

Larva: Along the Atlantic coast, larvae from spring spawning in the South Atlantic Bight are carried north by currents and spend the summer in estuaries of the Middle Atlantic sight (1399). Larvae hatched off Chesapeake Bay in summer are carried inshore south of Cape Hatteras (509 13991, and may spend a month or more in the estuaries in late summer (1399). Larvae occur mostly in surface waters, but probably move to greater depths as swimming abilities develop.

Juvenile: Kendall et al (1399) suggested that bluefish are estuarine dependent as juveniles.

Young of the year: move inshore sometime during first growing season and some are often found in estuaries and their tributaries (509 47 2 7  ) . In Texas, class 0 fish arrive in coastal waters during late November when 48-56 mm SL (322) and some evidently enter bay systems (255 47 550 574). In the Atlantic, juveniles are essentially shore fish that stay with the warmer water and frequently enter inner bays (421). Juveniles apparently move out of the estuaries in the fall, and move southward along the coast (1399).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae: Pelagic and planktonic (415 509).

Juveniles/adults: Pelagic and nektonic. A migratory species in which both large juveniles and adults school, but usually separately (791). Adults show a diurnal rhythm being active during the daytime (30 47 275 518 520 538 574 766 788). Swimming speed increases at light onset and decreases during the late afternoon and evening to a resting phase, although swimming never ceases (753).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Temperate and warm temperate zones, generally in continental shelf waters (766). Primarily oceanic and found both inshore and offshore (51 834). Young may enter bays, sounds, and rivers (834 1393)

Eggs/larvae: Found in offshore waters principally on the outer half of the continental shelf usually occurring midshelf and seaward. Captures occur mostly in the upper portion and surface of the water column, but larvae probably seek greater depths with growth and increased swimming ability. Young move inshore sometime during first growing season and occasionally they are found in the mouth of bays. Collected from water depths ranging from 34 to 183 m (30 47 509 415 481 766). Found in euhaline salinities (30 47).

Juveniles: Reported from both inshore and offshore areas in clear and turbid waters. Inshore habitats include ocean beaches, lagoons, sounds, bays, barrier island passes, estuaries, and bayous. Probably not estuarine dependent and only considered as a casual visitor to such waters, but movement into these areas may have survival value due to shelter and food resources (19 47 223 255 275 509 550 574 786 788 887). Found as far as 96 km offshore in ?fairly deep water? extending possibly to the thermocline with a reported depth range of 1.1 to 26 m (124 223 275 509 786), but both juveniles and adults have been reported in nearshore habitats in water as shallow as 0.15 m (1406). Juveniles have also been collected considerable distances up rivers in the New England area (509 275). Salinities from which juveniles are reported range from freshwater to euhaline (223 255 550 574 538 275).

Adults: Captured in nearshore areas of barrier islands and their passes, and along island beaches on the Gulf side, but are not common in low salinity estuaries. Adults may move into or near estuaries to feed (47 223 651 695); they have been collected in the Loxahatchee River, FL 2.5-3 miles inside of Jupiter Inlet (887). During spawning season, they have been reported up to 148 km offshore in the Mid-Atlantic Bight (509). Occurrence is possible in water as deep as 100 m (223 275 420).

Substrate: Juveniles have been found over bottoms of shell and sandy shell with hard packed mud (574 786). Bottom types for all life stages are probably many and varied due to the pelagic wide-ranging nature of this species.

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs: Eggs have been successfully incubated in a temperature range of 18-22.2C (average temperature 20.0 C) (177). Hatching occurred in 46-48 hours at a temperature of 20.0 C (177). Eggs in the wild occur from 18-26.30 C in the Chesapeake Bay area (509).

Larvae: Larvae have been collected in the Gulf of Mexico at temperatures ranging from 23.2 to 26.4 C (30 47). It was thought that bluefish larvae do not occur at temperatures below 21 C (889), but Kendall and Walford (1399) collected larvae in temperatures as low as 16.4 C in October. Nearly all the larvae that they collected between Palm Beach, FL and Cape Cod were taken in water temperatures between 17.0 and 26.0 C (1399).

Juveniles/adults: Juveniles have been reported in waters from 14.8 to 31.2 C (223 255 420 550 574 936). Water temperatures below 10 C are considered lethal for this life stage (421). The temperature range recorded for adults is 18-27 C (177 223 509 887 1400). Adults are never found in any numbers at temperatures lower than 15-50 C (51). Swimming speed is significantly affected by temperature, with stressful behavior noted at a low of 11.9 C and a high of 29.8 C (519). Adults can survive temperatures as low as 7.5 C for short periods (421), and they occur in nearshore areas of northeast and east central Florida where temperatures exceed 27 C for prolonged periods (1400). Reported as killed by freezes at Sanibel Island, FL (1068), but not reported as killed by freezes elsewhere in Florida (236 836 1023).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae: Eggs have been incubated at 32.5 ppt until hatching. Eggs in the wild occur from 26.6-34.9 ppt, but are found most frequently in 30 ppt or greater (509). Salinity range of larval collections is from 35.7-36.6 ppt (30 47).

Juveniles: Collected over a salinity range of 8.0-30.0 ppt in the Gulf of Mexico and from 0.0 to 37.5 ppt throughout their range (223 255 275 550 574).

Adults: Salinity preference appears to be 26.6 to 34.9 ppt (471, but they exhibit an overall range of 7.0-36.5 ppt with only rare occurrences above 35 ppt (177 223 255 275 651 887). Known to penetrate low salinity rivers on the Florida east coast (887).

Turbidity: Reported from turbid waters, but probably only as a stray because they are highly vision oriented (518 520 4 7).

nodes.title: Reproduction
nodes.body:
Repro Mode: Sexes separate, fertilization is external. No accessory organs present (766).
Mating and Spawning: Essentially offshore ocean spawners (415). Gulf of Mexico populations appear to spawn over, or seaward of, the continental shelf as they do in the Atlantic off the eastern U.S. (30 415 481 509). Spawning in the northern Gulf of Mexico seems to occur in the fall, from late September through early November (304 30 216), and 150-200 mm young have been caught in Tampa Bay in April (664). Spring spawning has been noted to occur in waters off the Louisiana coast (30). Spawning in the Atlantic has been known to occur 55-148 km offshore in salinities of 25.6 to 32.5 ppt, and water temperatures of 14 to 25.60 C (177 509 766 47). Kendall and Wolford (1399) found two areas of concentrated spawning in offshore waters of the Atlantic: one in spring on the western edge of the Gulf Stream in the South Atlantic Bight, and the other in summer over the continental shelf of the Middle Atlantic Bight. Larvae have been taken in every season of the year in offshore waters of the Atlantic coast (13991, but greatest larval concentrations off Chesapeake Bay occur in the summer months and spawning peaks in July (509). Optimal temperature and salinity for spawning were reported as 25.60 C and 31 ppt in the Chesapeake Bay area (509). Minimum temperatures and salinities at the onset of spawning reported as 180 C and 26.6 ppt (509). The majority of spawning in the Chesapeake Bay area is reported to occur at temperatures above 220 C and surface salinities of 31 ppt or greater (47 177 509 766).

Reproductive Capacity: Approximately 112,000-195,000 eggs are released during spawning by Black Sea bluefish (275). Number of eggs produced is a function of size and age (766). A 528 mm female contained about 900,000 maturing eggs while a 585 mm female contained about 1,100,000 eggs (766). Female bluefish weighing 1.9-2.7 kg contained 600,000 to 1,400,000 eggs (1399).

Growth and Development
Egg: fertilized eggs are all 0.90-1.20 mm in diameter and contain a single oil globule 0.22-0.30 mm in diameter (177 415). Perivitelline space is ca. 0.167 of egg radius. Cell division proceeds rapidly. Early morula stages occur 2 h after fertilization (AF) at 18-22.2; at 14 h AF, blastoderm envelopes one third of yolk diameter; by 20-30 h AF embryo enters tail-free stage; heart has developed and begins beating at about 34 h AF. Regular movements are first noticed at about 37 h AF with hatching occurring between 44-48 h AF at 18.0-22.20 C (177 415 509).

Larvae: Newly hatched larvae are 2.0-2.4 mm TL (177 509). Early growth is very rapid, but decreases after the third day (1392). Average length of larvae hatched in the laboratory given as 2.1 mm at hatching, 2.8 mm on day 1, 3.0 mm of day 2, 3.2 mm on day 3, and 3.3 mm on day 4 (177). Fin buds and urogenital duct appear on second day. Yolk-sac absorbed by about 4 mm TL. Incipient fin rays are evident by 6 mm TL and countable by 8 mm TL. Fin development complete by 13-14 mm TL marking end of larval stage (177 415 509).

Juvenile: Minimum length about 14 mm SL (415 509). Fish spawned in spring in the Middle and South Atlantic grew to about 200 mm FL by fall, and summer spawned fish were about 230 mm by the following spring and 290 mm that fall (766). Maturity occurs during the second year when fish are about 300-350 mm FL (177 766). A 200 mm TL female with nearly mature eggs was reported from Mexican waters (304). Testes mature slightly ahead of ovaries in fish of similar size (766).

Adult: Scale analyses have been used to determine that bluefish live until at least 9 years of age, but larger and presumably older fish that may be as old as 14 years have been reported (766). Sizes for different year classes range as follows; 230 mm FL at I+ year; 400 mm FL at 2+ years; 490 mm FL (1,816 g) at 3+ years; 580 mm FL (3,178 g) at 4+ years; 640 mm FL (4,086 g) at 5+ years; 690 mm FL (4,540 g) at 6+ years; and 710 mm FL (5,448 g) at 7+ years (766). A size of about 860 mm FL and 8,455 g has been suggested for fish reaching 14 years of age (766).

Lassiter (1393) presented von Bertalanffy growth equations, as well as the following equation expressing the length-weight relationship for North Carolina bluefish:
[eq]
W = (2.45 x l0^(-5)) (FLA2.903)
[/eq]
A similar equation for bluefish from South Carolina, Georgia and Florida was presented by Oliver et al (1392):
[eq]
W = (1.49 x l0^(-5)) (FLA2.985)
[/eq]
The length-weight equation for bluefish from the New York Bight, calculated by Wilk, Morse and Ralph, 1978 presented in (1392) is:
[eq]
W = (1.12 x 10^(-5)) (FLA3.036)
[/eq]
Maximum size reported as 1.0 m (327) or 1.1 m and 12 kg (788). Fish larger than 6.8 kg are rare (834), and reports of fish weighing 23 kg have not been verified (788).

Food and Feeding
This fish is a voracious, pelagic, marine feeder visually preying throughout the water column on a large variety of fishes and invertebrates, including various crustaceans and marine worms (47 51 518 520 766). Several authors characterize the bluefish as destructive, often killing many more of its prey species than they can consume (51 312 834). Young fish feed on copepods, crustacean and molluscan larvae, and fish fry (51 1393). Juvenile prey are of smaller size and include shrimp, squid, pinfish and silversides (1393). Adult bluefish are primarily piscivorous and invertebrates are progressively less important as fish increase in age (47 69 467 592 766 1393 1407). Wilk (766) presented a comprehensive list of the food of bluefish from the Atlantic
Coast which includes 16 invertebrate and 67 vertebrate species.

Ecological Interactions and Notes
Populations off the U.S. coast are not homogenous, but are thought to be composed of six races (420 421). This is supported by the homing tendencies of this fish and tag return data (421) .

Only sharks, tunas, swordfish, and Wahoo pose threats as predators to these fast swimmers (766). Bluefish are in competition for food with other high level predators including Morone saxitilis, Scomberomorous maculatus, S. cavalla, and large Cynoscion SPP

Parasites and disease: This species is particularly vulnerable to finrot. Known parasites include isopods, copepods, cestodes, trematodes, nematodes, and protozoans ( 766 ) .

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
September 3, 1993.  T.D. Phillips; Mote Marine Laboratory

FLELMR Code: 1609

Common Name: Bluefish
Scientific Name: Pomatomus saltatrix
Other Common Names: blue (664); greenfish, tailor, snapping mackerel (312 834); snapper (51); skipjack (834); elf, fatback, snap mackerel, horse mackerel, skip mackerel, chopper, Hatteras blue (766 1392).

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
Class:     Osteichthyes
Order:   Perciformes
Family:  Pomatomidae

sections.heading: Value
sections.content:
Commercial: Considered an incidental commercial species with most catches occurring in offshore waters (30 47 420). They were once common enough to support a small fishery in east Texas waters, but not since the 1930`s (255 320). In Alabama they are a relatively minor component of that state`s commercial fishery (694). Catches there are largely by trammel nets in waters off the Gulf beaches, but in recent years shrimp trawls have made up 25% of the catch (694). Statewide Florida landings in 1989 were 1,250,718 lbs worth approximately $318,249, and of that total, almost 67% were landed at Florida east coast ports (902). Catches are also made by pound nets, gill nets, purse seines, long haul seines, beach seines, and hook and line in other areas of the range of this fish (753 791 834). Marketed mostly fresh (791).

Recreational: An important sport species in both U.S. and Mexican waters. Its recreational importance far outweighs its commercial value especially on the Atlantic seaboard (30 47 420 304 695). Their voracity makes them an exciting game fish and they are also an excellent food fish (51 327). The recreational catch for 1991 for the Florida Gulf was estimated as 430,000 fish, and on the Florida Atlantic coast as 856,000 fish (1363). Angling methods include surf casting; hook and line fishing from piers, docks, bridges, and jetties; and trolling, casting, live bait fishing, and chumming from boats (51 753).

Ecological Role: A marine, high trophic level, pelagic predator that is primarily a visual feeder (518 520 766). Follow schools of small fishes into shallow water and are known to have bitten bathers (788 1406).

Indicator: Bluefish bioaccumulate contaminants such as polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB) from the water column and through the marine food chain into various adipose tissues (618). Studies by the National Marine Fisheries Service, the Food and Drug Administration, and the Environmental Protection Agency have found concentrations of PCBs in large bluefish that exceed the limit of 2 pg/g set by the Food & Drug Administration. This has prompted investigation to determine if states with bluefish fisheries need to control the consumption of large individuals to recreational and subsistence fishermen who regularly eat these fish ( 618 ) .

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content: Overall: Worldwide in distribution (327 766 788 791 887 891). In the western Atlantic from Nova Scotia to Argentina, and widespread in the Gulf of Mexico to Texas and Mexico (420 766 791). It is also found off Cuba, Bermuda, and the Azores (791 891). Rare or absent between south Florida and northern South America (788). Much less abundant overall in the Gulf of Mexico than in the Atlantic, and generally less common on the western side of the Gulf than the eastern (753).

sections.heading: By State
sections.content:
Within Study Area: Occurs on both coasts of Florida (327 581 789 791 887 891). Abundant along the northeast Florida coast (1392) and common in winter and spring in the Jupiter Inlet area (887).  Caught offshore in the Gulf during most of the year (6641, and known to occur in relatively large numbers offshore of Cedar Key (581). Not common on the Florida west coast during the winter (581). Historically, known to be common near Pensacola (978).

Movements and Migrations
Adults: move seasonally in groups loosely collected into aggregates (766) that can be 6-8 km long ( 5 1 ) . Adults generally move north in spring and summer, and south in fall and winter (766 481). Long distance migrations from New York to Cuba, and from Virginia to the Florida Gulf coast have been documented ( 5 1 275). Florida blue fish remain in Florida waters until spring and large numbers are still found off southern Florida in March; some are present throughout the year (177 553 327 664). In the Gulf of Mexico, they remain offshore during much of the year moving inshore during the summer in Louisiana, late summer and fall in Mississippi, and fall in Florida and the northwestern Gulf. Seasonal migrations appear to be linked to water temperature and possibly photoperiod (519 766). Fall migration appears to be triggered when temperatures fall to 13-150 C. Adults are pelagic fish and move offshore to find warmer water in which to overwinter (421 766 581). Movements between offshore and inshore
waters are irregular and may be a response to wind induced changes in water temperature (421 766 581).

Larva: Along the Atlantic coast, larvae from spring spawning in the South Atlantic Bight are carried north by currents and spend the summer in estuaries of the Middle Atlantic sight (1399). Larvae hatched off Chesapeake Bay in summer are carried inshore south of Cape Hatteras (509 13991, and may spend a month or more in the estuaries in late summer (1399). Larvae occur mostly in surface waters, but probably move to greater depths as swimming abilities develop.

Juvenile: Kendall et al (1399) suggested that bluefish are estuarine dependent as juveniles.

Young of the year: move inshore sometime during first growing season and some are often found in estuaries and their tributaries (509 47 2 7  ) . In Texas, class 0 fish arrive in coastal waters during late November when 48-56 mm SL (322) and some evidently enter bay systems (255 47 550 574). In the Atlantic, juveniles are essentially shore fish that stay with the warmer water and frequently enter inner bays (421). Juveniles apparently move out of the estuaries in the fall, and move southward along the coast (1399).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Eggs/larvae: Pelagic and planktonic (415 509).

Juveniles/adults: Pelagic and nektonic. A migratory species in which both large juveniles and adults school, but usually separately (791). Adults show a diurnal rhythm being active during the daytime (30 47 275 518 520 538 574 766 788). Swimming speed increases at light onset and decreases during the late afternoon and evening to a resting phase, although swimming never ceases (753).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type: Temperate and warm temperate zones, generally in continental shelf waters (766). Primarily oceanic and found both inshore and offshore (51 834). Young may enter bays, sounds, and rivers (834 1393)

Eggs/larvae: Found in offshore waters principally on the outer half of the continental shelf usually occurring midshelf and seaward. Captures occur mostly in the upper portion and surface of the water column, but larvae probably seek greater depths with growth and increased swimming ability. Young move inshore sometime during first growing season and occasionally they are found in the mouth of bays. Collected from water depths ranging from 34 to 183 m (30 47 509 415 481 766). Found in euhaline salinities (30 47).

Juveniles: Reported from both inshore and offshore areas in clear and turbid waters. Inshore habitats include ocean beaches, lagoons, sounds, bays, barrier island passes, estuaries, and bayous. Probably not estuarine dependent and only considered as a casual visitor to such waters, but movement into these areas may have survival value due to shelter and food resources (19 47 223 255 275 509 550 574 786 788 887). Found as far as 96 km offshore in ?fairly deep water? extending possibly to the thermocline with a reported depth range of 1.1 to 26 m (124 223 275 509 786), but both juveniles and adults have been reported in nearshore habitats in water as shallow as 0.15 m (1406). Juveniles have also been collected considerable distances up rivers in the New England area (509 275). Salinities from which juveniles are reported range from freshwater to euhaline (223 255 550 574 538 275).

Adults: Captured in nearshore areas of barrier islands and their passes, and along island beaches on the Gulf side, but are not common in low salinity estuaries. Adults may move into or near estuaries to feed (47 223 651 695); they have been collected in the Loxahatchee River, FL 2.5-3 miles inside of Jupiter Inlet (887). During spawning season, they have been reported up to 148 km offshore in the Mid-Atlantic Bight (509). Occurrence is possible in water as deep as 100 m (223 275 420).

Substrate: Juveniles have been found over bottoms of shell and sandy shell with hard packed mud (574 786). Bottom types for all life stages are probably many and varied due to the pelagic wide-ranging nature of this species.

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Eggs: Eggs have been successfully incubated in a temperature range of 18-22.2C (average temperature 20.0 C) (177). Hatching occurred in 46-48 hours at a temperature of 20.0 C (177). Eggs in the wild occur from 18-26.30 C in the Chesapeake Bay area (509).

Larvae: Larvae have been collected in the Gulf of Mexico at temperatures ranging from 23.2 to 26.4 C (30 47). It was thought that bluefish larvae do not occur at temperatures below 21 C (889), but Kendall and Walford (1399) collected larvae in temperatures as low as 16.4 C in October. Nearly all the larvae that they collected between Palm Beach, FL and Cape Cod were taken in water temperatures between 17.0 and 26.0 C (1399).

Juveniles/adults: Juveniles have been reported in waters from 14.8 to 31.2 C (223 255 420 550 574 936). Water temperatures below 10 C are considered lethal for this life stage (421). The temperature range recorded for adults is 18-27 C (177 223 509 887 1400). Adults are never found in any numbers at temperatures lower than 15-50 C (51). Swimming speed is significantly affected by temperature, with stressful behavior noted at a low of 11.9 C and a high of 29.8 C (519). Adults can survive temperatures as low as 7.5 C for short periods (421), and they occur in nearshore areas of northeast and east central Florida where temperatures exceed 27 C for prolonged periods (1400). Reported as killed by freezes at Sanibel Island, FL (1068), but not reported as killed by freezes elsewhere in Florida (236 836 1023).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Eggs/larvae: Eggs have been incubated at 32.5 ppt until hatching. Eggs in the wild occur from 26.6-34.9 ppt, but are found most frequently in 30 ppt or greater (509). Salinity range of larval collections is from 35.7-36.6 ppt (30 47).

Juveniles: Collected over a salinity range of 8.0-30.0 ppt in the Gulf of Mexico and from 0.0 to 37.5 ppt throughout their range (223 255 275 550 574).

Adults: Salinity preference appears to be 26.6 to 34.9 ppt (471, but they exhibit an overall range of 7.0-36.5 ppt with only rare occurrences above 35 ppt (177 223 255 275 651 887). Known to penetrate low salinity rivers on the Florida east coast (887).

Turbidity: Reported from turbid waters, but probably only as a stray because they are highly vision oriented (518 520 4 7).

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.content:
Repro Mode: Sexes separate, fertilization is external. No accessory organs present (766).
Mating and Spawning: Essentially offshore ocean spawners (415). Gulf of Mexico populations appear to spawn over, or seaward of, the continental shelf as they do in the Atlantic off the eastern U.S. (30 415 481 509). Spawning in the northern Gulf of Mexico seems to occur in the fall, from late September through early November (304 30 216), and 150-200 mm young have been caught in Tampa Bay in April (664). Spring spawning has been noted to occur in waters off the Louisiana coast (30). Spawning in the Atlantic has been known to occur 55-148 km offshore in salinities of 25.6 to 32.5 ppt, and water temperatures of 14 to 25.60 C (177 509 766 47). Kendall and Wolford (1399) found two areas of concentrated spawning in offshore waters of the Atlantic: one in spring on the western edge of the Gulf Stream in the South Atlantic Bight, and the other in summer over the continental shelf of the Middle Atlantic Bight. Larvae have been taken in every season of the year in offshore waters of the Atlantic coast (13991, but greatest larval concentrations off Chesapeake Bay occur in the summer months and spawning peaks in July (509). Optimal temperature and salinity for spawning were reported as 25.60 C and 31 ppt in the Chesapeake Bay area (509). Minimum temperatures and salinities at the onset of spawning reported as 180 C and 26.6 ppt (509). The majority of spawning in the Chesapeake Bay area is reported to occur at temperatures above 220 C and surface salinities of 31 ppt or greater (47 177 509 766).

Reproductive Capacity: Approximately 112,000-195,000 eggs are released during spawning by Black Sea bluefish (275). Number of eggs produced is a function of size and age (766). A 528 mm female contained about 900,000 maturing eggs while a 585 mm female contained about 1,100,000 eggs (766). Female bluefish weighing 1.9-2.7 kg contained 600,000 to 1,400,000 eggs (1399).

Growth and Development
Egg: fertilized eggs are all 0.90-1.20 mm in diameter and contain a single oil globule 0.22-0.30 mm in diameter (177 415). Perivitelline space is ca. 0.167 of egg radius. Cell division proceeds rapidly. Early morula stages occur 2 h after fertilization (AF) at 18-22.2; at 14 h AF, blastoderm envelopes one third of yolk diameter; by 20-30 h AF embryo enters tail-free stage; heart has developed and begins beating at about 34 h AF. Regular movements are first noticed at about 37 h AF with hatching occurring between 44-48 h AF at 18.0-22.20 C (177 415 509).

Larvae: Newly hatched larvae are 2.0-2.4 mm TL (177 509). Early growth is very rapid, but decreases after the third day (1392). Average length of larvae hatched in the laboratory given as 2.1 mm at hatching, 2.8 mm on day 1, 3.0 mm of day 2, 3.2 mm on day 3, and 3.3 mm on day 4 (177). Fin buds and urogenital duct appear on second day. Yolk-sac absorbed by about 4 mm TL. Incipient fin rays are evident by 6 mm TL and countable by 8 mm TL. Fin development complete by 13-14 mm TL marking end of larval stage (177 415 509).

Juvenile: Minimum length about 14 mm SL (415 509). Fish spawned in spring in the Middle and South Atlantic grew to about 200 mm FL by fall, and summer spawned fish were about 230 mm by the following spring and 290 mm that fall (766). Maturity occurs during the second year when fish are about 300-350 mm FL (177 766). A 200 mm TL female with nearly mature eggs was reported from Mexican waters (304). Testes mature slightly ahead of ovaries in fish of similar size (766).

Adult: Scale analyses have been used to determine that bluefish live until at least 9 years of age, but larger and presumably older fish that may be as old as 14 years have been reported (766). Sizes for different year classes range as follows; 230 mm FL at I+ year; 400 mm FL at 2+ years; 490 mm FL (1,816 g) at 3+ years; 580 mm FL (3,178 g) at 4+ years; 640 mm FL (4,086 g) at 5+ years; 690 mm FL (4,540 g) at 6+ years; and 710 mm FL (5,448 g) at 7+ years (766). A size of about 860 mm FL and 8,455 g has been suggested for fish reaching 14 years of age (766).

Lassiter (1393) presented von Bertalanffy growth equations, as well as the following equation expressing the length-weight relationship for North Carolina bluefish:
[eq]
W = (2.45 x l0^(-5)) (FLA2.903)
[/eq]
A similar equation for bluefish from South Carolina, Georgia and Florida was presented by Oliver et al (1392):
[eq]
W = (1.49 x l0^(-5)) (FLA2.985)
[/eq]
The length-weight equation for bluefish from the New York Bight, calculated by Wilk, Morse and Ralph, 1978 presented in (1392) is:
[eq]
W = (1.12 x 10^(-5)) (FLA3.036)
[/eq]
Maximum size reported as 1.0 m (327) or 1.1 m and 12 kg (788). Fish larger than 6.8 kg are rare (834), and reports of fish weighing 23 kg have not been verified (788).

Food and Feeding
This fish is a voracious, pelagic, marine feeder visually preying throughout the water column on a large variety of fishes and invertebrates, including various crustaceans and marine worms (47 51 518 520 766). Several authors characterize the bluefish as destructive, often killing many more of its prey species than they can consume (51 312 834). Young fish feed on copepods, crustacean and molluscan larvae, and fish fry (51 1393). Juvenile prey are of smaller size and include shrimp, squid, pinfish and silversides (1393). Adult bluefish are primarily piscivorous and invertebrates are progressively less important as fish increase in age (47 69 467 592 766 1393 1407). Wilk (766) presented a comprehensive list of the food of bluefish from the Atlantic
Coast which includes 16 invertebrate and 67 vertebrate species.

Ecological Interactions and Notes
Populations off the U.S. coast are not homogenous, but are thought to be composed of six races (420 421). This is supported by the homing tendencies of this fish and tag return data (421) .

Only sharks, tunas, swordfish, and Wahoo pose threats as predators to these fast swimmers (766). Bluefish are in competition for food with other high level predators including Morone saxitilis, Scomberomorous maculatus, S. cavalla, and large Cynoscion SPP

Parasites and disease: This species is particularly vulnerable to finrot. Known parasites include isopods, copepods, cestodes, trematodes, nematodes, and protozoans ( 766 ) .
